On motion of Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 64,. to amend the Indian Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Will of Indian devising property to. be approved; land devised or bequeathed to non-resident on the reserve to be sold:

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Will the minister kindly explain this section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: As the law stands now, an Indian cannot devise his interest in the band property to any other than a member of the band. It frequently happens that his very close relatives are members of another band. This Bill will enable an Indian to devise his interest in the band property to any one outside of the band, but when that happens the- Superintendent General is empowered to sell the devised property and distribute the proceeds to the heirs.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Do I understand that an Indian will be able to devise his land to. any other person, even if that person is not an Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: He can devise in any way as set out in 'section 25 of the Indian Act. There is a restriction in that clause to the effect that the testator cannot devise or bequeath land in a reserve or any interest therein-unless to his daughter, sister or grandchildren-to any one not entitled to reside on such reserve. Consequently, his rights to bequeath are in no way restricted by this amendment. They are enlarged, but only to such extent as to enable him to bequeath to the same class of people, even though they do not inside in that reservation.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: They will have to be Indians, though?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
No. The Superintendent General may sell the property devised to any other member of the reservation, and distribute the proceeds to whom it was bequeathed. That is to say, the heirs get it, but they do not get it in the form of

land, because if they did they would have to go upon the'reservation. They get it in the form of proceeds.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: No matter whether the heirs are white or not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: The law is not changed in that particular. There is no wider range given at all, except to the extent of enabling them to bequeath to heirs outside of the reserve. There is no change in the nature of the Act.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: It has been enlarged, because formerly, if I understand correctly, no .devise or bequest could be made to any one not entitled to reside on the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: So it would have to be an Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Under this change, the Indian will be able to leave his property to anybody, but such land will have to be sold, and the proceeds given to the heirs. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I have not made myself clear. The class of people to whom the Indian may devise is not altered at all.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Is that class defined in the Indian Act?
Mr. 'MEIGHEN: Section 25 of that Act reads as follows:
Indians may devise or bequeath property of any kind1 in the same manner as other persons :	Provided that no devise or bequest of
land in a reserve or of any interest therein unless to the daughter, sister or grandchildren of the testator, shall be made to any one not entitled to reside on suoh reserve, and that no will purporting to dispose of land in a reserve or any interest therein shall be of any force or effect unless or until the will has been approved by the Superintendent General, and that if a will be disapproved by the Superintendent General the Indian maiding the will shall be deemed to have died intestate; and the Superintendent Generali may approve of a will generally and disallow any disposition thereby made of land in a reserve or of any interest in such land, In which case the will so approved shall have force and effect except so far as such disallowed disposition is concerned;
The only alteration made is this: that whereas under the present Act "no devise or bequest of land in a reserve or any interest therein unless to the daughter, sister or grandchildren of the testator, shall be made to any one not entitled to reside on such reserve"-that restriction is removed. He may bequeath to others even though

they do not reside on the reservation, provided, of course, that the will is approved by the Superintendent General. But if he does bequeath to others who do not reside on the reservation the land must be sold and the proceeds only go to the devisees.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Where an Indian has married >a white woman, and has died without heirs, is the wife entitled to any interest in the land belonging to the hand? Supposing the members of the band tried to send her away from the land belonging to her husband, and she wished to remain, is she entitled to.remain there or not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the amendment, but the law of the matter is covered by section 26 of the Act. If the hon. gentleman reads that section, which is a very long one, he will see what becomes of the property of an Indian who dies intestate.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: The object is to leave the reserve intact for the band?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes and to give wider liberty of bequest.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-proof of assent to release or surrender.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Before whom was the oath formerly taken?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: An attempt had been made to particularize; various additions were made from time to time, yet the provision seemed still to be insufficient, because many of the officials designated as persons before whom the oath could be taken were not within reach. We simply wish to provide an omnibus clause so that any one who can take affidavits in the province is competent to take an affidavit in this case. Notaries were not included in the list. We want the section simply to read: "Any person having authority to take affidavits and having jurisdiction within the place where the oath is administered."

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Indian may be summoned as witness:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: In a certain investigation Indians were advised by some ingenious lawyer not to appear, and he made out a very strong case that they were not " persons " within the meaning of the Act. We wish to avoid lawyers' fees in any further cases of that kind.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-direction of expenditures of capital of band without consent:

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The powers conferred
by this section upon the Superintendent General appear to be very wide. As long as its deputy head is such a competent official as Mr. Scott, I have no objection, but we cannot always have Mr. Scott.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: The powers' go only to the extent of enabling the Superintendent General to arrange for the cultivation'-not for the expropriation-of Indian lands for the benefit of the Indians'.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I refer the hon. gentleman to the first subsection of this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
That merely provides
for the utilization of a >share of the capital of the band for purposes looking to the. improvement of the conditions of the band and their property, not to the taking away of any of their property.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I understand that if the band feel that the money should be used in a certain way, that the Superintendent General, who is the guardian of these wards of the nation, may decide to follow another course. Of course, the Governor in Council would not do anything contrary to the interests of the band. But these are very wide powers. I should have no objection if Mr. Scott were eternal, ibut unfortunately he is not.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Under the old Act,
no such action could be taken as is contemplated by this section without the consent of the- hand. The Superintendent General could not expend the capital money of the band without their consent, even for the cultivation of the land or the improvement of the reserve. To this first section, I think, there is mo objection; but subsection 3 provides that the Superintendent General shall have the right to grant a lease of lands in the reserve to a third party. May this not *lead to serious trouble between the Indians and such third party? The Indians might object very strongly to strangers going on their reserve, even with a lease 'from the Government, to cultivate their land. This is a very important change. Previously nothing of this kind cduld be done without the consent of the band.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The departmental
officials do not anticipate that trouble. Still, the hon. gentleman has a very correct appreciation of the change that has been effected in the law. It is putting it out of ,the power of what one may call reaction-

ary or recalcitrant. Indian bands to cheek their own progress by refusing consent to the utilization bl their funds or vacant lands for their own advantage. The hon. gentleman is not quite right in his understanding that at present no such power in any respect is given to the Superintendent Generial. It is, in these two respects: Fo,r purposes, for example, of surveys or of drainage, the consent of the Band has already been dispensed with, or rather provision has been made that it may be dispensed with. We are simply extending that principle. It is necessary to do so now, particularly, in view of the production campaign that we have under way throughout the Indian Reserves of Western Canada. The Indian Reserves of Western Canada embrace very large areas of land far in excess of what they are utilizing now for productive purposes. We have well under way in that country a campaign _for the utilization of those reserves, for stock raising, -for grain production, and, for the present, of course, in many cases, merely for summer fallowing. But we do not want to have this campaign entirely at the mercy of the Indian hands themselves. We do not want to have those bands stand in our way and say to us: Notwithstanding the necessities of to-day, you must keep off all this vacant land unless we choose to give it u,p to you and ourselves forego the great privilege of roaming on it in its old, wild state. We want to be able to utilize that land in every case; but, of course, the policy of the department will he to get the consent of the band wherever possible, and to meet the bands in such spirit and with such methods as will not alienate their sympathies from their guardian, the Government of Canada. We do not anticipate that we shall come into very serious conflict with any band. It is'only the more backward bands that offer any objections at all to the utilization of their land.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
In the case of a very
large reserve in which the band has been reduced to very small numbers, is there any clause in the Bill making it possible for the department to appropriate a portion of their land-actually to take it out of t their hands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: No, only to the extent of enabling us to lease it, paying them the fair rental value of it, less the value of the permanent improvements. The title is not taken away.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The question of leasing
Indian lands has just come up. On_ what terms are those lands leased? This is the first year in which the question of enormously increasing production has been discussed. Many persons .have asked me for information in regard to the matter, and I have never received authoritative information. On what terms are the lands leased to actual settlers'and stock Taisers, and for what period of time are they leased? What goes with the lease as regards fencing? Will the department fence the land and charge a certain rental according to the number of head of cattle per acre?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I cannot, for very obvi-oug reasons, give the hon. member any information as to terms. The commissioner under whose supervision all this work in the West is being done is Mr. W. M. Graham, late inspector and agent at File'Hills. Mr. Graham has been in the service of the Indian Department for between thirty -and thirty-five years. He has made a most conspicuous success of his Indian settlement work and of his management of the agencies under his control. The Order in Council which gives him his powers is very wide. It necessarily was wide. It would otherwise have been .impossible for us, at this end, with proper expedition, to fix_the terms in any individual case. Mr. Graham is given power to make leases himself on behalf of the department, subject, of course, to our approval. We depend upon him to get the best terms possible. We do not as yet know what terms he is able to secure. I have from him an intimation that, in respect of one reserve in which already there are existing rights, he is securing a per-head basis very substantially in excess of the per-head basis that we get from those who now have existing rights. It was his anticipation that he would get very substantial rentals in each case. It must, however, be kept in mind that his paramount object is to eeciire productive results, at the same time, of course, securing fair and adequate returns to the bands for the rental values of their lands.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I wish to commend the minister for this section in the Bill. In the very centre of the district which I represent there is a large Indian reserve, possibly the most productive section of that country, served with railways and having every market facility. I should like to see this provision go further so as to allow the minister to give those lands for cultivation purposes as well as for grazing, because at this time, when we require

so much production, lands adjacent to a market and a railway are much more advantageous for purposes of cultivation than those further back from business centres.
I have listened to what the minister has said in regard to the powers of Mr. Graham.
I have spoken to Mr.. Graham in connection with his work in Western Canada. The only criticism I might make of his work there at the present time is that I am afraid he is going to get from the rental of those lands more money than they are worth. At a time when we need every effort put forth for the purpose of increasing the stock of this country as well as for the purpose of grain production, Mr. Graham, as I learned from my last conversation with him, is getting more for the grazing privileges of an Indian reserve than, in my judgment, the farmer can afford to pay. This, of course, is for the benefit of the Indians, and, from that point of view, no exception can be taken to it.
I hope the minister will allow, or instruct, Mr. Graham to do all he can to lease this land on, say, a five-year term for the purpose of cultivation, because there, are thousands of acres of land that are immediately adjacent to markets ' and that are lying absolutely idle and of no value whatever either to the Indian or to any one else.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Does not this provision include cultivation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I was just going to say so. It includes provision for leasing for cultivation.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Under the old Act, I understand, the Government and the Indian could lease a quantity of land for the term of one year for the purpose of cultivation. Under this Bill does the Government expect to make a lease for a term of one, two or three years?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is wrong. Previously we could lease for any term within the scope of the surrender obtained from the Indian band.
There was no limitation to one year, and similarly, there is no limitation now. I believe that the leases are being made for three years, and possibly in some cases five years, the intention being to cover at all events the period of great need caused by the war.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
fs the consent of the
whole band required or only the consent of the owner of the part leased?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
If the man were the recognized owner of the part leased he alone
would have to be dealt with, but if the pro- ' perty belonged to the band the consent of the band would have to be obtained in compliance with the Indian Act.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the department to make any provision for the Indians in cases where the larger part of the reservation is leased?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The Indian is very fortunate; he has all he had before, and now in addition he has the rental for this land.
I do not think we need waste any time in sympathy for the Indian, for I am pretty sure his interests will be looted after by the Commissioner.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: The Indian has only got now what we left to him after confiscating what we wanted. Now we are proposing to, take the balance of the rights we then reserved to him. The Indian may ask to be allowed to live on this land which he leases to the Government, but under this Act he will not be permitted to do so if the Government wish otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I cannot agree with the hon. member that there has been any confiscation at all. I believe that the Indians of this country have been liberally and generously dealt with, and I believe it is the intention and spirit of the country to 'continue to treat them generously. That spirit is evidenced by this Act. Where the Indian does not cultivate his land we are providing that we may arrange for its cultivation, the title still remaining in the band. The Indian gets the benefit of that cultivation by way of rental.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: But we are taking away his right of residence on the reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Suppose it is decided to lease an entire reservation, would the Indians still be allowed to trap and hunt over the reserve or would they have to leave the reserve entirely?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: We do not provide for that. We provide only for leasing the uncultivated part. Of course, if there are no Indians on the reservation we might lease it all, but that is -not what my hon. friend fears; he fears the Indians will be put off. They will never be put off under this Act, which only provides for leasing the unused areas.	.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Are these shortterm leases?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Is it the intention under this Act to expropriate the land that is not heing cultivated and lease it to other parties who will use it for grain growing or grazing purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The 'intention is to
lease it without expropriation.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: It is practically the same thing. Then what becomes of the Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: He gets the benefit of all the cultivation that he has heretofore undertaken and the benefit of all the land that he has been using for grazing, and all the other benefits coming to the Indian under the law. Now we are providing an additional benefit by giving value to what had no value to him before.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
But will the Indian be
allowed to trap and hunt if the entire reservation is taken? If not, where will he go?
iMr. MEIGHEN: We will still leave him enough to trap on, but even if we did not thirty bushels of wheat to the acre is a lot better than a few squirrels caught by the Indian.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say that the land would Joe leased for the purpose of raising grain as well as stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does not understand the commissioner as well as I do, or he would not have made the statement which he has made. I have known the commissioner for thirty years, and I may say there is not a more competent officer. He will never permit any company, syndicate or individual to use the lands in any such manner as the hon. gentleman suggests. One reason why I support the Bill which the minister has brought in is because it gives Mr. Graham so much latitude. I know that the interests of the country and of the Indians will be properly looked afteT in his hands, and if there should happen to be any using of these lands in the manner suggested, he will quickly take the necessary steps to terminate the lease. I have been over a good many of the Indian reserves, and I know something about the hundreds of acres of land lying idle. I know that if any lease is terminated at any time for any cause hundreds of farmers would be only too glad

to take the lease and work the farm successfully. It is all veTy well to say you should give all this land over to stock-raising. If the land were suited for it, that proposition would be perfectly good, but unfortunately, there lare millions of .acres of land in "Western Canada in which grain raising is exclusively indicated and where ' stock raising would not be a success. A great deal of this land is of that nature. Therefore, I say, it is a perfectly propeT thing today to give a free hand to Mr. Graham, and let him use the land for grain raising, if it can be so used, and use such parts for stock raising that are as suitable. I have no hesitation in saying that this whole question of handling the Indian reserves is very properly placed in the hands of the 'Indian Commissioner, Mr. Graham, and it will be properly looked after.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I did not say anything
regarding Mir. Graham, I know him by reputation but not personally, and I may say no better officer is in the employ of the country than Mr. Graham, but that does not affect what I said in regard to the renting of the land. He cannot control every man who uses that land. What would happen if he died? Somebody would have to take his place, and perhaps we would not get -as good a man as Mr. Graham. Another point is that this land could not be used for stock raising, because a great deal of it is only adapted for grain raising.. Any land that will raise grain will raise stock, but a great deal of land that will iraise stock will not raise grain.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I have the honour to represent a constituency where there is a . large-sized Indian reserve, and a number of the Indians on that reserve already own their land. The farmers adjacent to the land owned by these Indians are renting the land [DOT] year afteT year and producing grain on it. I know further that that same reservation has a lot of the very best land in the country on it for grain purposes, hut it is not suitable for stock raising because the water is not available. In order to raise stock your land must be adjacent to water, but you can grow wheat where you have not the opportunity of obtaining water. I have great pleasure in endorsing this measure.
Mr. J. S'. REID:	I congratulate the
Minister of the Interior for going as far as he has gone. I know a great many Indian reserves. In the province in which I live thousands of acres are lying idle, and
farmers having ranches alongside these reserves are only too glad to get leases of this land to raise grain and cattle. Perhaps there is a danger here that when we make an Indian a landlord and he rents out his land, he will sit back with his hands in his pockets and receive his rent, and it will tend to make him a little lazy. In regard to the land being polluted with noxious weeds, I do not think there need be any fear. That matter cap be attended to. As to production, we have many Indian reserves in Saskatchewan lying quite close to our railway towns, and I am sure this measure will greatly stimulate Droduction. J am very much in sympathy with the amendment to the Act.
Mr. 'CAHILL: If the onlv Durnose of the Bill is to deal with vacant land, there are thousands and millions of acres of vacant land throughout the West owned by large corporations, and why we should take from *the Indian his rights, where he is living on the land in his own way, to make way for settlers or renters, and leave to the large corporations their, lands which they are holding for profit, is a mystery to me. fl think if we are going to do any confiscating of land for the beRefit of the white plan, you should take the white man's land.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	Under subsection
3, when these lands are rented or leased, is there provision for a tender?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Not necessarily, because there would not be time to tender in every case.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I do not wish to be misunderstood, and I may say I am not in favour of confiscating the Indian land, because I know by the last returns the Indian population is increasing, and there may he a day when the Indians will require all the land. But leasing and confiscating are different propositions.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: It depends on how long you lease the land for.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
night it would be absolutely impossible for him to cultivate more than a small fraction of these lands. In regard to raising stock on all these lands, the Indians would be unable to do it. They would not be able to finance themselves. Some criticism has been made of the production of grain. Some lands are not suitable for growing grain and some are suitable only for that purpose. If a man can farm successfully in any part of the Dominion, he can do so on the lands of those Indian reserves. In the early days when they were set apart, they were not accessible by railway. In the southern portion of Alberta there is the Stony Indian reserve, through which the railway now passes. The railway runs within five miles of the Sarcee reserve. It also passes right on the edge of the Blackfoot reserve, in which there are some of the finest agricultural lands .in Canada. The Blood reserve *at Cardston is in close proximity to the railway.
If a man can farm and make a success of it in Alberta he can certainly be successful on any of these reserves. It is hindering the development of the country to have this land withheld from cultivation. What affects the West affects every other part of Canada. I am sure that what is being done by the Government this year in opening up portions of these reserves will assist very materially in, increasing the output of grain in these three western provinces. I think this amendment is entitled to the support of every member of the House, there being no question of the confiscation of Indian lands in it.	[DOT]

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
May I make reference to one part of the section that has not yet been referred to? This discussion, so far, has been based upon the question of leasing, but if I apprehend the rest of this section, it goes to this extent that the commissioner may speculate with the funds of the band to the extent of making improvements. If there are proceeds from such improvements, the hand is ahead of the game, but if he has had the success that I have had as a lawyer in speculating in farming, makes a botch of it and loses money, the band would be out that much. I think this part of the section might more seriously concern the House than what we have been discussing as to leases. I am not much concerned about leases because they will bring in something, but when it comes to making improvements at the expense of the band it is something that must be considered be-

cause the band deserves the protection of this House.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) is rather apprehensive. There is no idea of speculating with the Indian fund. Subsection 2 provides that the capital fund of the band may be used for the improvement of the Indians' property. There is no intention of going further than that. Already we can do that for purposes of drainage, surveys, etc. The Indian is the ward of the Government still. The presumption of the law is that he has not the capacity to decide as to what is for his ultimate benefit in the same degree as has his guardian, the Government of Canada. Consequently, it has been affirmed that the fund of the band should be, and can be, used, with or without his consent, for the purposes I have named. This only goes to the extent of extending the principle further and enabling us to use the funds of the band for the purpose
9 p.m. of making improvements to the Indians' property. That is all, and that clearly appears by subsection 2. In subsection 3, we have provided that we may lease and cultivate unused land. It may be that the hon. gentleman fears that, if we cultivate it, we may not cultivate it to advantage, that is. to say, that we may lose money. But the Indian gets the fair rental value of the land. We are not speculating with his property; we give him the fair rental value. Consequently, the Indian cannot complain; and the country cannot complain because this is an attempt on a sound basis to increase production; and I do not think, therefore, that the House should further hesitate.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I do hot think the people of the country would complain so

much if provision were made for tenders. As my hon. friend from Neepawa (Mr. Davis) pointed out .a minute ago, you could speculate with this land. Some friend of the Government may get some of this land. I think it is bad policy to depart from the tender system, and I do not think that the reason given by the minister a minute ago, that he had no time to do what wais suggested, is a good reason. If there is no time this year, this land should only be rented for one year. The rights of the Indians should not be interfered with unless there is grave reason for so doing. This is a drastic measure, and the reason for it given by the minister is not sufficient.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have not the fear that some of my hon. friends have that the Indian will be interfered with. I believe, as the minister states, that the Indian will be better taken care of under some such system as this than he will be ifvhe is left entirely to his own resources. I come now to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders), who swung all around and about what I said and then had to come back and admit the truth of my statement, that if you rented this land to first-class; practical farmers, it would be very much better. I would say, take all the Indian lands, leave the Indians enough for purposes of habitation, and pay them a rent for what you take. If you are going to rent land, if you are going to do it in a hurry, and if you are going to do it without tender-and it was done without advertisement only two weeks ago-you are going to see Jim, Jack and the other fellow take it up wrhile the prices of wheat and all grains are high, and then desert it, with the. result that the country will be the loser. 'I do not quite agree with my hon.. friend (Mir. IDuTremblay) when he says that the minister should rent the land ~ for one year. I do not think that is fair. Take, for instance, the case of a stock man. He probably takes a section of land, he buys up 500 sheep, puts them on the land and if it were proposed to put him off the land at the end of the year it would not be fair. Neither would it be fair to a man who is entirely a grain grower and who. with the best of intentions, would start in and buy up horses, tractors, binders and other things, if he were only allowed to keep the land for one year. The minister and the. department should take every precaution, as I am sure they will, to protect the people as well as the Indian. He should protect the neighbours of the people who are farming these lands as well as the people who are on the lands and, of course, the people of the country generally. I am satisfied that as far as Mr. Graham is able to do it, the work will be well done, but Mr. Graham is not infallible by any means any more than the rest of us. I am not opposing this measure but I am trying to improve it. It is a good move. The Indian, on the whole, will be better off; but, at the same time, let us see that the Indian, the department, and the people, are given every protection. 'There is no need of rushing into a thing and making a botch of it. If we are going to take it up let us do it right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: As to tendering, I am sure that Mr. Graham would call for tenders in every case where there is time and where the circumstances permit. There are large reserves where there are certain rights already, where it may be found well to lease a certain permit or privilege over a certain section of it, or perhaps found well to rent part of it for grazing, and so on. Under conditions of that sort, it does not appear to me that tendering is possible. It may be that some of the land will be leased to friends of the Government. . In that very prosperous and intelligent country from which we from the West come they are all friendly to the Government, so that it is a contingency we cannot avoid. But it will be leased honestly all the same. I know there is a great deal in what the hon. member says, that land temporarily leased for cultivation and thereafter abandoned" is very likely to deteriorate through weeds. That consideration has prevented us leasing school lands, and I have had to stand a good deal of abuse of the opposite kind to that to which I have been subjected to-night because we refused for that reason to lease school lands. But in this case the lands leased are those oveT which we have a system and machinery of direct supervision. We have an agent at every reserve, with sufficient power in his hands to supervise the leasehold, and if it should be that the land should be under cultivation for a time, and then no longer under cultivation, at least we will have the benefit of the fencing in the meantime, and then we can apply the method of farming which the hon. gentleman suggests; we can put the cattle on after that, because the fences are there, and they will take care of the weed situation in very little time.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
I would like to ask in regard to - the leasing of Indian reserve land to farmers who will crop this land.

Will it be possible for the land so leased to come under the municipal law of the different provinces, so that the machinery of the municipal law will have effect?
Mr. MBIGtHEN:	That question is more
than ordinarily difficult. iMy impression is it would not come under the provincial law.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Would it not toe better if it did?
Mr. MEI'GHEN: I could not answer very well, because I do not know what the provincial law is in the province referred to by the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: In all municipalities in Saskatchewan there is a weed inspector who looks after noxious weeds.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Yes, I think these
leases will toe subject to that law.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Will it be the policy of the Government to have the land cultivated under the direction of the Superintendent General with the money of the Indian band when no lease is granted? The Government will have that authority under subsection 2 of section 4. The Superintendent General is authorized to expend the capital moneys of the band for the purpose of cultivating or improving the land, even wimout the consent of the band. I think there is danger of the condition arising referred to by the Ijon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis). If the operations ,are not successful financially, the Indians will be the losers as a result of that expenditure. The Superintendent General himself could have the land cultivated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Certainly. But the Act provides that if we do, we give the Indian the fair rental value of the land leased, less such of the moneys as have gone into permanent improvements, of which, of course, he gets the benefit.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Not under subsection 2.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: No, under subsection 3.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes, but under subsection 2 the expenditure ef the capital moneys of the band is authorized for the purpose of improving or cultivating the land. There is no provision that the Indian shall receive nothing. Of course, he will receive something if the operations are successful, but if they a.re not he will lose as . a result of the expenditure of that money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: It is not the purpose to expend the capital moneys on anything except permanent imipTovements, and the Act provides that -these shall toe only for such purposes as may be considered reasonable and proper. Then subsection 3 clearly indicates that the purpose of the expenditure of the capital funds is for permanent improvements only. In case we use the land, we- pay a fair value.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: If I may be permitted I would like to ask the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) what he thinks might become of the Indians on the Sarcee reserve when this Bill comes into force? About how much of the reserve, is under cultivation at the present time?

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The effect of this Bill
will certainly be that the capital fund of the Sarcee Indians will be increased, because thousands of acres in that reservation which are not under cultivation, which are not being used for grazing purposes, and which are not producing one single cent to the Indians, will then be producing revenue. Under this system the Indians are bound to receive some money, and if the Government follows the policy of leasing the land to independent tenants, then the Indians receive that money without the expenditure of one single cent, and the general revenue of their capital fund will be increased to the extent of these rentals. On the other hand, if the Government spend money on the cultivation of the land, the Indians then will be in the same position, I take it, as an independent farmer, and if a profit is made out of the crop, as the Sarcee Indians made last year and the year before in raising grain, then their capital fund will be increased to that extent. It is a profit-making transaction from almost every angle from which you look at it. There is this possibility, that, if they invest their money in seed grain or build a fence, they get no revenue from the fence other than the protection of their crop. If there should be a frost, or hail, or a drought, there will be no crop, and they will lose the cost of their seed grain, and they will have put in their own services and their own energy, which will be lost to them, just as would be the case with any other farmers under similar conditions,

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
But will the Indian of
the Sarcee reserve be satisfied? There is only a small acreage on that reserve under cultivation. The greater part is partially fenced, very poorly fenced, part of it. But the whole of it is fenced now.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The reserve contains something in the neighbourhood of 70,000 acres. Will the Indians be satisfied that they are being treated fairly? Will they accept the conditions we are laying down, or are they dissatisfied?
' Mr. TWEEDIE: Well, the Indian may be satisfied and he may not. My personal view with regard to the Indian is that he is the ward of the Government, and being a ward he is bound to accept the treatment given him. The treatment of the Indian should be the very best that can be offered him under the circumstances. But it seems to me that it is no part of the treatment of the Indian to allow thousands of acres of land to stay out of cultivation and not put to use for grazing purposes. It seems to me that the position of the Indian as a ward is almost the position of any other ward, and that the guardian of that ward is bound to exercise his judgment, as the Minister of the Interior points out, in the best interest #of the ward. When we produce revenue for the benefit of the Indians themselves out of land which is now lying idle, I think that is the treatment which should be accorded to the Indians; and I believe it to be the duty of this Government to make use of the Indian lands for the benefit of the Indians themselves.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: It seems to me that this enactment is designed for the purpose of benefiting farmers whose land adjoins Indian reserves. It is not reasonable that an inroad should be made on Indian reserve lands in the West until the other lands throughout that country have been 'taken up. There is something in connection with this enactment which does not seem square to the Indians. The Indians are the wards of Canada, and deserve every consideration at our hands. I think that we should not too hastily approve this legislation.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: I have heard it stated outside the House that the department fences the land and then leases it to a rancher, who puts on the land so many head of cattle per acre. Does the department fence the land and then lease it, or does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
It is usually provided in the lease that the lessee shall fence, but under section 90 of the Act, as amended by this amendment, the department has power to fence and to charge the cost to capital account as permanent improvement. The cultivation could then be done and rental
paid to the band on a fair value basis. In order to make it clear that no capital fund shall be used except for permanent improvement, I move:
That dtfter the word "in" in the sixth line of section 4 there he inserted the words "subsection 1 of."
Subsection 1 clearly sets out that the improvements shall be permanent.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: The Government are doing the right thing in protecting not only the general public, but their wards as well. But the Government have other, landed wards who own, control, and hold out of use large tracts of land in'Western Canada -I mean the big interests. What is the Government going to do about them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: We feel that they are quite capable of taking care of themselves.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-taxation of dogs, protection of sheep:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
The object of this
clause is a very useful, though not a very lofty one. It is to provide for the curtailment of the privileges of Indian dogs. The Superintendent General is empowered to make by-laws for the taxation, control and destruction of dogs and for the protection of sheep; and such by-laws may be applied to such reserves or parts thereof as from time to time the Superintendent General may direct. For many years complaints have been made of the depredations of Indian dogs, particularly in the destruction of sheep. We have had no way of dealing with the matter. The Indians had power tb make by-laws which would be ratified, if necessary, by the Governor in Council; but the Indian is very sensitive on the subject, ,and does not move very rapidly along the path of civilization in this respect. We want to take care of this dog question.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
No penalty has been provided?
M'r. MEIGHEN:	Yes, the penalty can
be fixed under the by-law.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-enfranchisement of Indians :

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Does this apply to all
Indians in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Certain bands of
Indians in Ontario have large oapital funds under their control. In many cases the Indians are farming outside of the reserves, and have been, perhaps by common consent, allowed to vote. I understand that, according to legal terms, the 'word " may " means " shall," and I have no doubt that if this clause is passed and comes to their attention, many of these Indians will ask for and be entitled to receive their share of the capital funds. I do not think it is in the interests of the country that these shares should be paid to them, especially in cases where the amounts are large. The Superintendent General knowrs the cases which I have in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: There is nothing obligatory on the Superintendent General. The Indian must not only be willing to surrender his interests and receive his share of the capital funds, ibut he must make application to be enfranchised; he must h.avie ceased to follow the Indian mode of life, and, most important of all, he must satisfy the Superintendent General that he is selfsupporting and fit to be enfranchised. Similar provision was made in the Act heretofore, but it was hedged around by this restraint: that before an Indian could have the privilege of establishing his right to enfranchisement he had to be a landed Indian. That is to 'say, he had to be in possession of a share of the landed estate of the band. There developed a great number of cases. I have in my hand a long list of Indians who are self-supporting, who follow various lines of life, being druggists, constables, professional singers, actors, missionaries, religious teachers, and so forth, but who, having no landed interest in the reserve, cannot come within the provisions of the Act, and therefore cannot be raised to the status of citizens. This provision is to remove that restraint.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-illegal celebrations:

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext: Will the minister tell us what those illegal celebrations are which are prohibited by this section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND CO-ORDINATION OF EMPLOYMENT OFFICES.
speechtext:
Section 149 of the Indian Act says:	[DOT]
Every Indian or other person who engages in, or assists in celebrating or encourages either *directly or indirectly another to celebrate any Indian festival, dance or other ceremony ot which the giving away or paying or giving back of money, goods or articles of any sort forms a part, or is a feature, whether suoh gift of money, goods or articles takes place, before, at or after the celebration of the same,

or who engages or assists in any celebration or dance of which the wounding or mutilation of the dead or living body of any human being or animal forms a part or is a feature, is guilty of an indictable offence.
We simply make this an offence subject to proceeding by summary conviction, in order to avoid the* expense of proceeding by indictment.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, amendments read the second time and concurred in.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. T. A. -Crerar (Minister of Agriculture), Bill No. 55, to amend the Meats and Canned Foods.Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-establishment:

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the difference between this and the old Act?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
This clause, -as it stands in the present Act, reads as follows :
"Establishment" means any abattoir, packing house, or other premises in which such animals are slaughtered, or in which any parts thereof or products thereof, or fish, or fruit, or vegetables, are prepared for food- for export or are stored for export.
The amendment to this section is the addition of the following words after the word " vegetables ":
Or any food or food product which may be named by the Governor in Council.
making the clause read as follows:
"Establishment" means any abattoir, packing house, or other premises in which such animals are slaughtered, or in which any parts thereof or products thereof, or fish, or fruit, or vegetables, or any food or food product which may be named by the Governor in Council, are prepared for food for export or are stored for export.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the idea *of the amendment?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why does the minister confine the provisions to export? '

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The amendment is simply an enlargement of the scope of the clause. It provides that any food or food product which may be named by the Governor in .Council may be added to those foods enumerated in the clause as it originally stood.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I presume this refers to " boiled dinners " and that sort of thing. Canned mixed-food is exported by several factories, and I presume this refers particularly to them. Mixed food put up

in cans is what is called " boiled dinners." (Does not the minister know about that?
Mr. iGRHRiAlR: I believe the clause could bt used to cover that.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The minister, I understand, says that this is an amendment to the Act, and the Act already provides for places for the preparation of food for home consumption. This amendment applies, only to places in which food is prepared for export.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Meat and. Canned Foods Act was intended to apply only to the foods enumerated that were intended ,for export or for interprovincial trade. I think the point to which the hon. gentleman refers is covered by municipal and provincial inspection, that is, in relation *to foods that are manufactured, say, at the point in which they are consumed. This Act does not apply to such foods, but if such foods are shipped either for export pr for interprovincial trade, it does apply to them.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Exports or imports of uninspected articles:

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I may explain that at present the regulations apply only to exported foods; they do not cover imported foods of a similar character. Their purpose, I am told, when originally passed, was to set a standard for Canadian articles exported to foreign markets, in order that we might establish a reputation abroad. But there is this curious anomaly, that there are no similar restrictions on foods imported into Canada, with the result that foods can be imported into this country without any (supervision as to their quality. We are now asking for power so that the department may require proper certification of the foods imported into Canada.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Who will carry out this inspection, and where will it be done?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is intended to have the customs officials do it. When the goods are entered for import into Canada these officials will see that the proper certificates are attached.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	Is the certificate
furnished by the American or by the Canadian inspector?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The certification will have to be satisfactory to the Veterinary Director General or to the Minister of Agriculture, who may accept certification of United States Government officials as to the wholesomeness of the foods manufactured in that country.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There has been a good deal of talk, and I have no doubt the minister has heard something of it, about the quality of the canned fruit and vegetables put up by our canners for the army. Is there any inspection of these factories at the present time by the Dominion Government? If there is no inspection, there certainly should be.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There is an inspection by the officials of the Department of Agriculture. The inspector is not located permanently at the point of manufacture, but he can drop in at any hour of any day and examine the goods in the process of manufacture. The British authorities have instituted a very rigid system of inspection of all canned goods for shipment abroad for army purposes. The other day, when we were discussing the resolution on which this Bill is founded, reference was made by an hon. member to a case at Belleville. Curiously enough, I have received a letter from this manufacturer, who had seen the reference to his factory in the newspapers. I have confirmed by inquiry the following, taken from this letter:
The facts are that all the vegetables manufactured in Canada for the British, French and United States Governments are rigidly inspected first by the IMilton Hersey Company, whose headquarters are in Montreal, and who have a very highly trained staff of officials. They place in every factory where these goods are manufactured one or more inspectors sufficient to examine every pound of vegetables before they are manufactured, also during the processing, and after they are manufactured and packed. They stamp every package and every case and every sack in which these goods are shipped or transferred from the manufacturing sub-station to the central packing depot, and nothing can be delivered! without the above regulation. The hills of lading and invoices have also to toe all stamped toy these officials. Then 20 per cent, of the invoice is withheld toy the British War Office until the goods reach destination and, have passed through a rigid1 examination and chemical analysis in France, which usually takes about four months after the goods are shipped from Canada, before we receive our pay.
That is>
the inspection that is carried on by the British Government officials of articles for army purposes. In addition to that, the officials of the Department of Agriculture carry on an inspection which is intended to cover all goods for export.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The reason I asked was that there was a gentleman here the other day who had a very interesting story to tell about some of these packing houses, and I think he is going to make it public some



of these days; it will certainly be interesting to the members and to the minister, and I have no donbt his story is correct. He was accusing the factories of putting up ' stuff that was not fit to pack.
Mr .CRERAR:	I have not, as full an
acquaintance with, this inspection as I intend (to have when I am a little longer in the department. While the inspection is not as perfect as it would be if an inspector were located permanently in each factory to *inspect every ounce of vegetable entering into the manufacture of these foods, nevertheless I think it is sufficient to afford a pretty fair check on their quality.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is the department taking any measures for inspecting small factories? There are quite a number of these small factories all over the Dominion, particularly in my province, putting up such foods as I mentioned a few minutes ago-" boiled dinners," which is a mixture of vegetables and meat, a well-balanced ration. These factories are up against very grave difficulties be1 cause they are not large enough to be entitled to an inspector. The Government provides that there must be an output of $50,000 or $60,000 worth of goods before an inspector will be appointed for the district. The result is that the small factories are put out of business by not being able to secure inspection. Has the Government received correspondence on that subject, and are they going to take measures to overcome that difficulty, and enable the small factories to compete with the big industry?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I will look into the point. I aim not aware that we have had any correspondence on the subject; I shall make inquiry concerning it. I want to point out, however, that this inspection does not govern in regard to goods consumed in the province where they are manufactured. It concerns only factories which are manufacturing goods for export, or interprovin-ciu.1 trade, and such factories, iif they are down in the province the hon. gentleman comes from, have the same facilities for inspection as other factories in other parts of the country.

Section agreed to.
On Section 17-False marking as to name.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is there provision in the law for marking the true weight and contents of packages? Subsection 2 provides that no false information concerning the contents of a package should be given.

I notice on many packages coming from the United States, the words: "This package contains so many ounces," or so many pounds, " exclusive of the package." It seems to me perhaps a rather wise provision to insert, in order that the public may be protected and know that they get what they are paying for.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Before replying directly to the question, I may say that the only change in this section is the provision that it shall apply to imports as well as exports. There is no provision, as far as I know, for marking on the label the exact weight of the contents of the can. The section merely provides that no package shall be marked with any label, brand or mark which will falsely represent the contents.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is it not the intention to apply the inspection to food for local consumption under the Act? I think it would be a wise provision.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No. This Act is intended to apply to goods manufactured for export or interprovincial trade. The regulation as to the purity of the goods manufactured for local consumption is left to the municipal or provincial authorities', and they have charge of the enforcement of the Adulteration Act, which provides the necessary machinery for protection in the case the hon. gentleman refers to.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think the hon. minister is perhaps not quite correct about The Meat Act applying to goods for provincial use. I think the three Maritime Provinces are included in one section. You cari export a carcass of pork which has not been inspected from one part of the Maritime Provinces to another, but you cannot export it to Quebec or Ontario.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may be right, but I cannot say definitely.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I wish to draw the hon. minister's attention to subsection 2, which reads:
(2) No package containing any article subject to inspection 'under tihis Act shall be marked with any label, brand or mark which falsely represents the quantity or weight or contents of such package.
In the West we get a very large quantity of canned tomatoes, and, as far as I know, they come very largely if not altogether from somewhere in Ontario. I do not believe we get any from Prince Edward Island. I have not noticed the stamp on the brand, but we certainly get a large quantity of water and a very small quan-

tity of tomatoes in these cans. I hope this measure will apply to canned tomatoes.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is this Bill intended to cover all the fish products, as well as other food?
* Mr. CRERAR: I understand, under legislation passed last year or the year previous, that the same provision applies to fish products, but the administration of that part of the Act is under the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Section 17 applies to all fish.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It applies to fish but that is under the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, and read the third time and passed.

maintopic: SUPPLY.

speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Customs-Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including ipay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, and' temporary Customs buildings and rentals, $3,890,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. L. SIFTON (Minister of Customs) :
maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
The amount of these estimates is exactly the same as last year. There has been a transfer of $25,000 from one column ,to another but the total is the same.
Mr. MicMASTER: The cost of collecting ,the customs revenue has been raised very considerably during the last six years, not merely taken as a whole, but pro rata. I would be glad to know if the minister has any hope to hold out to us that it will not require so much to raise the revenue as has hitherto been found necessary.
IMr. SIFTON: I have shown evidence of pot intending to raise the amount by only asking for the same amount as was voted last year. 1 have hopes that by a rearrangement of some of the work I may be able to make the relative amount, comparing it with the work that is done, less than it has been at some times in the past.
Mr. MoMASTER,: In the county that I know most about, it cost about twice as much the year before last to raise the customs revenue as it did during the year 1911-12. I never heard that the officers were over-worked. I remember having the figures for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1916, before me and they showed that there
67}
were about twice as many officers, and that about twice as laTge an amount in salaries was paid during that year as in 1911-12. I draw the attention of the minister to this fact because we are in hopes that in this era of economy we may see a very substantial improvement. I think there is room for it in certain parts of the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
I will take great pleasure in looking into the conditions existing in my hon. friend's county to ascertain if there is the extravagance of which he complains. It does not go through the whole service, because in looking over the lists of salaries I do not think they are at all commensurate with the amount of work dene. But if anything of that kind is found to exist in my hon. friend's county, I will try and see that the customs officers in tliat county shall be kept down to a reasonable rate if he insists upon it.
Mr. MoMASTER: I do not want the minister to labour under any misunderstanding. I am not complaining so much abopt the rate; of salary that is paid as the fact that it takes now about nine men to do the work that five did before, and although the nine men belong to the party that used to be called the Conservative party and the five who formerly occupied these positions belonged to the Liberal party, I do not think that the difference in intelligence would account foT the fact that it takes nine men now to do the work that five did before.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
Are the five still there?
Mr. MoMASTER: No, the five disappeared, of course.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: In the minister's Teply to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) he left the impression that this extravagance in the customs service was confined to one county in the Dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: All I said wasdliat that was the first case that I had heard of.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
I think that perhaps' eveTy other member representing a constituency in this Dominion would say the same thing as the hon. member for Brome does. I do not wish to criticize the minister, because he has only been in charge of the department for a few months, but if he will investigate the work of the department at the different customs ports in all parts of Canada he will find that the service is overmanned and that hundreds of thousands of dollars could be saved. I would ask the minister to make an investigation during the coming 'Summer, and I venture to say

he "will find a great many customs offices where there are twice as many men employed as are necessary to do the work.
'Mr. EDWARDS: I doubt very much the accuracy of the statements made toy the hon. gentleman (Mr. Duff), who has just taken his seat, and toy the hon. member for Brome. It may toe that there are certain localities where the salaries paid in proportion to the revenue collected are greater than they were a year or two ago, tout, without having the figures before me at the present moment, I venture the assertion that during the last fiscal year, taking the Dominion over, it costs less per dollar, or per hundred dollars of revenue for collecting than it did in previous years. I doubt if the hon. member for Brome can substantiate the statement that the cost pro rata is greater than it was a year or two ago.
